html:
A huge public bath complex in the south of Rome, built about 212 to 216 under Septimius Severus and his son Caracalla. It held some 1,600 bathers at a time and was the city's largest baths until the Baths of Diocletian.

It was more like a leisure center than a bath. Visitors moved through cold, warm and hot halls, swam in an open pool and exercised in courtyards. There were gardens, and Greek and Latin libraries. A branch of an aqueduct fed it, and furnaces under the floors heated the water and rooms.

The baths ran for about three centuries. They ended in 537, when the Goths besieging Rome during the Gothic War cut the aqueducts. The ruins later yielded great statues such as the Farnese Bull. The vast vaulted halls also inspired modern buildings, among them the old Pennsylvania Station in New York.
